#46752. I coach four-time Grand Slam champion Aryna Sabalenka. Here’s why winners shouldn’t always focus on speed

I coach four-time Grand Slam champion Aryna Sabalenka. Here’s why winners shouldn’t always focus on speed

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for years, I was always a step behind on the jujitsu mat.
  • Industry observers note that for years, I was always a step behind on the jujitsu mat.
  • Recent findings suggest that then one day, time slowed down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for years, I was always a step behind on the jujitsu mat. I’d rush, scramble, and attack from poor positions. I was reacting to my opponent’s game plan, not mine. In the end, I was defeated. Then one day, time slowed down. I was present, maybe even a little ahead of the moment. My partner was relentless in his attack, but I wasn’t chasing him. My heart rate and breathing settled. When he moved, I was a step ahead. The first thing you learn on the mat isn’t how to win. It’s how to defend. That moment was a result of years of drilling defense. It provided me room to breathe, adapt, and attack based on MY game plan. Jujitsu changed forever for me that day. My coach, Jhunior Guarnido, teaches it as a process: Defend, Control, Attack. It starts as a sequence you cycle through, but as you improve, it becomes one continuous forward motion. Defense and Control are built into the Attack. You want to act without hesitation, but never lead by pure emotion, reckless behavior, or your opponent’s timeline. Defend, Control, Attack gives you the freedom to play to win. If the Attack isn’t going to plan, you flow through the sequence and begin again. This is how winners operate. I’ve coached Aryna Sabalenka for eight years but also work with founders and executives. When they’ve felt pressure, most go straight into an attack. I love that. Wanting to dictate the pace and outcome is what winners do. The problem is their awareness and timing. Before you see what’s really happening, you move from a bad position, often from fear or a forced reaction on a clock someone else set. Why the early attack backfires A good jujitsu opponent will always push you to rush. They’ll count on you to react to the pressure and make a mistake. Markets do the same exact thing. One of your competitors reveals a new AI on Monday and the press calls it a game changer. How does your board react? They’re asking you where yours is. By the next day, you’ve pulled together a team, stalling momentum elsewhere, and promised a made-up launch based on your competitors’ schedule, not yours. The feature introduces without being fully tested, your customers notice, and internally, frustration grows. Just like my early days on the mat, you’ve been rushing, scrambling, attacking from a poor position. You call it action, but your team feels the panic and chaos. Rather than acting from a solid base, where trust and conviction are built, you’ve acted from fear. What it looked like in Sabalenka’s 2025 season Aryna is one of the most relentless competitors I’ve ever been around. She’s a four-time Grand Slam champion who spent more than 100 weeks as World #1. But in 2025, at both the Australian Open and French Open finals, the titles got away from her in deciding moments. Her Attack was already the best on tour. So we had to cycle through Defend and Control to identify the limiting factor. We soon identified the Control phase as that factor, so we worked on her internal state. That meant revisiting breath control, listening to her gut, and learning to adapt without rushing. We worked on controlling the pace and dictating the match. By September 2025, she was holding the US Open trophy. The same thing happens in business I coached a young, ambitious entrepreneur named Brad, who seemed to be at the top of his game. He knew every detail about the operations of his tech giant. His approach was the opposite of Aryna’s: all defense, no attack. He was preparing for a meeting with a potential investor, the kind of meeting that could change his business forever, and he prepared in the way he always did. He created scripts and frameworks, and had an answer for any possible question. While Brad had memorized all this information, it left him no room to adapt or make connections. His timing was always off, and the investor could feel it. This is why we started working together; he had too many missed opportunities. We didn’t work on his business, we worked on HIM. We reviewed his Defense and cycled through Control and Attack. Defense: His knowledge was impenetrable. But he was manipulated by his own preparation, unaware of his own weakness for any given moment or environment. Control: He lacked awareness and was unable to read the room. He missed moments to connect and build trust. Attack: His attack was always forced, getting stuck in his rehearsed script and poor positioning. To improve his Attack, we had to build his Control through breathing, movement, and sleep the week before a substantial meeting. Yes, Brad was right to know his business inside and out, but he needed to listen to his gut, not his head, and leave space before responding to a challenge. Staying in control of HIS state allowed him stay steady and present, then direct the conversation to his key points. In the end, the investor chose not to partner with him. But he was so impressed with Brad that he made a connection with someone he thought would suit him perfectly. That connection changed everything, doubling his revenue that first year. He now leads a team of his own coaches, providing him the freedom to take control of not only the business but his life. How to reset in the middle of a bad week When you find yourself a step behind, pressured to rush into a decision, it can be overwhelming, especially as a leader with people counting on you to lead. But leading from fear isn’t constructive for your organization. Here’s my advice when you find yourself in this situation: Begin the Defend, Control, Attack sequence. Defend: What slipped this week? Did you change your sleep or your diet? What data was overlooked? Maybe you fell into a trap you didn’t see coming. Close the obvious openings and don’t feed the panic you’re feeling. Frame it to build your base for control. Control: Whose urgency is this, really? What matters this week? Where do you want to be standing by Friday? Attack: Make the call. Have the conversation you’ve been putting off. If it doesn’t land, you’ve got a base to come back to. The leaders I admire and trust most under pressure still Attack, just like Aryna. But they do it from the position they’ve chosen to be in. While everyone around them is reacting to pressure, they find themselves a step ahead. That opening is often one they’ve created through their own sequence.

Gemini rolling out 66 latest regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (431 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following a preview at Google I/O, Google is rolling out 66 upcoming regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today.
  • For consumers in the UK, the enhancement brings over 10 distinct English voice options covering a wide range of regional cadences.
  • Sources indicate that this might help reduce the issues that sometimes still occur when English accents, in particular, morph into a hybrid of Australian or even American that has been going on for a while with Gemini Live.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a preview at Google I/O, Google is rolling out 66 upcoming regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today. The expansion introduces tailored voice options across U.S. English, U.K. English, Indian English, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, Indonesian, and Korean.

For consumers in the UK, the enhancement brings over 10 distinct English voice options covering a wide range of regional cadences. The lineup includes Geordie, Scouse, Brummie, Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish, Modern RP, and Multicultural London English (MLE).

Sources indicate that this might help reduce the issues that sometimes still occur when English accents, in particular, morph into a hybrid of Australian or even American that has been going on for a while with Gemini Live. We have not yet been able to test to confirm this has been resolved with the enhancement. As someone with a regional English accent, this extra representation with Gemini voices is quite welcome.

Recent findings suggest that according to Google, these voices are tuned for natural pronunciation, pitch, and everyday local rhythm rather than exaggerated stereotypes. Because the focus is on cadence over slang, Gemini will sound like a local without filling its text responses with forced street slang. Once selected, your chosen voice carries across the entire app, applying to both Gemini Live conversations and standard text-to-speech playback when tapping the “Listen” icon on chat responses.

You can preview and select the new options today by tapping the three-dot menu inside Gemini Live, or by heading into the Gemini app settings and selecting “Gemini’s voice.” It’s worth noting that the voices aren’t explicitly labeled by city or region in the app menu, and Gemini isn’t programmed to self-identify which accent it is using if you ask it directly.

In a recent development, instead, Google notes that locally rooted prompts about food, culture, or sport, such as asking for the best pub in Sheffield for a Sunday roast – my suggestion is not a pub; it’s Turnip & Thyme on Eccleshall Road, FWIW. Or another suggestion from massive G is where to find proper ingredients for a traditional Scouse stew; the company notes these will naturally bring out the warmth and rhythm of the latest dialects.

I’d suggest trying to ask where to get the best pattie and chips in Hull or where to get the best pint in Leeds (it’s Whitelocks).

Agentic shopping is creating a crisis for marketers. Here’s how to fix it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Understanding your customer is the foundation of marketing.
  • Understanding your customer is the foundation of marketing.
  • In a recent development, for more than two decades, we built the internet to filter bots out, and we were right to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Understanding your customer is the foundation of marketing. What drives decisions? What does the person in front of you respond to? What makes them choose you? Those questions sit at the back of every marketer’s mind when designing a campaign. So what is a marketer supposed to do when the customer turns out to be an AI agent? For more than two decades, we built the internet to filter bots out, and we were right to. Now many of the ones arriving at a website are not really bots at all. They are customers in a upcoming form. Tens of millions of Americans already trust a personal AI assistant, such as Meta’s Muse or Instinct, to book, buy, and arrange aspects of their lives for them. Meta told investors on its last earnings call that more than 10 million people in the United States and Canada had set up Muse agents within six weeks, that a quarter of them use it daily, and that the average purchase runs above $200. Those people are not browsing. They are delegating. Websites are reporting record numbers of visitors as these artificial intelligence assistants move across the internet at machine speed, working through a task someone gave them. The marketing reflex has been to filter harder. These are not real visitors, the thinking goes, and we need a way to tell AI agents apart from customers. Telling them apart does matter, though not for the reason most people assume. If a business keeps blocking AI assistants, it loses in two different ways. The first is immediate. AI systems are built to finish the task they were given. An assistant that runs into a wall on your site does not file a complaint or abandon the errand. It moves to the next site that enables them to complete their task, which is very likely a competitor’s. The customer who sent it never finds out you were an option. The second is slower and harder to reverse. These agents generate feedback as they work, and that feedback shapes what the next generation of models knows about the web. A business an assistant could never complete anything with does not sit at the top of that context. It is remembered, if at all, as somewhere not to bother trying. The floor, not the goal Letting agents in is the floor rather than the goal. The more interesting work is happening at companies that are not simply opening the door but deciding, deliberately, what an assistant may do once it is inside, where a human has to approve a step, and at which point in a process a person must take over. My organization scanned 2,053 organizations to test what an AI assistant sent by a customer could actually accomplish on their site. Just 2% have built a way for a customer to authorize an assistant with access they can limit and withdraw. None have reached the top level of readiness, where agents are a supported channel across web, interface, and voice. Consumers, meanwhile, have already made their decision. They are handing assistants real money and real tasks, and the usage numbers are not ambiguous. The next competitive ground is going to be at the agent level, and in the agent language, as businesses compete for the attention and the ease of use of software, rather than people. A new digital channel is opening, and marketers will have to build a strategy for appealing to something with no eyes. That is not a figure of speech. Every digital channel that marketers have learned in 30 years assumed a person at the other end. Someone looks at the page, reads the headline, feels something about the imagery, and decides. Search, social, display, and email all rest on that assumption, but it has stopped being reliably true. The gap this leaves is enormous. Of the organizations we measured on whether they have built something an assistant can actually act upon, the average score is 2.5 out of 100. Just 2% percent publish a product catalog a machine can read. Just 7% have published any position at all on whether assistants are welcome. The companies doing best are overwhelmingly software businesses, which score 57.7 on average against a field average of 38.8, not because software is clever, but because it is already built for machines reading machines. There is a risk in doing nothing, and it is not the one most marketers would guess. When a page became outdated, a promotion ended, or a referral program expired, the practice was to archive it or take it out of the navigation and move on. An assistant does not navigate. It reads what is there, and a page hidden from a menu is as findable as the homepage. Some 23% of the organizations we scanned had a file published telling an assistant what is current and what it may use. For the rest, an assistant can return to its customer with an offer that expired two years ago, presented as though it stands today. A question of intent Set against all of this is the part that should make marketers genuinely interested rather than merely anxious. An assistant arrives carrying intent. Not a referrer and a bounce rate, but a direct and specific statement of what a customer wants, delivered before the customer gets there. No channel in the history of marketing has handed anyone that. A business able to hold a conversation with an assistant learns exactly what the person behind it is looking for. Only 7% of the organizations we scored can connect to an assistant at all, and it is reasonable to assume those 7% are pulling ahead in a competition before their rivals even realize it exists. None of the work required here is exotic. Publish a product catalog a machine can read. Publish a file that tells an assistant where things live and what it may do. Give customers a way to authorize an assistant for a narrow task, with access they can withdraw. Decide, deliberately and in writing, whether agents are welcome, rather than leaving a 20-year-old configuration to answer on the brand’s behalf. And then, treat the result as a channel, which means tracking why these visitors arrived, what happened when they did, and how many converted into customers. The reason to treat this as urgent rather than interesting is that positions in this channel are being allocated right now, quietly, according to which businesses an assistant can actually finish a task with. Marketers spent the mobile transition arguing about whether the site needed to be responsive while competitors built things that worked only on a phone. This shift is further along than it looks, and the companies winning it are not winning with better creative. They are winning because an assistant could read them.

  • Nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs.
  • Industry observers note that the bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “upcoming in 621.14,” which came out on Nov.
  • According to recent reports, the “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs. One user measured about 3GB an hour on the susceptible driver, and another mentioned estimated up to 30GB/hour on the newer 621.24. This follows a similar-looking bug from AMD’s video driver discovered last month.

Industry observers note that the bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “upcoming in 621.14,” which came out on Nov. 4, who states it operates by “continuously [rewriting] the binary log file” with “real writes” to the drive. The writes are coming from the NVDisplay.Container.exe process, or the “NVIDIA Display Container LS” service, which logs to the nvlog.nvlgstg file. This background service is necessary for running the Nvidia Control Panel and App. It’s not clear what’s written in the log, and not every system is necessarily impacted.

According to recent reports, the “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive. The measurements came from Windows Resource Monitor, Windows performance counters, and CrystalDiskInfo. The Data Units Written counter matched Windows’ reporting. This test highlighted 515MB of process I/O coming with 270MB of total writes to the C: drive over five minutes. That works out to roughly 3GB per hour, in line with the user’s own estimate.

Worse, “the write volume increases as the file grows.” Stopping the service and deleting the log can temporarily reduce the writes. With the previous driver version 621.01, the writes totaled less than 2MB per five minutes, and a second user in the thread confirmed that a rollback helps.

Mitigation attempts, such as three clean reinstalls with the help of DDU from that second user, did not fix the problem. The writing process also impacted gaming and video performance, potentially causing hitching, which suggests it gets worse under load.

Another user, AyzekUorren, in a separate thread about driver 621.24, which came out Nov. 12, says that it could get up to “about 30gb per 1h” or even “70gb or even more” with longer sessions. This is even with telemetry disabled in the Nvidia App. Noted is that every Alt+Tab added 500MB to 1GB of writes, at least for this user.

It has been revealed that in AMD’s case, it was the External Events Utility, or atieclxx.exe, that exhibited constant writes on an idle PC. In that case, the AMD utility was reportedly copying its own executable every second. To put the impact into context, the AMD bug had rates reported between 0.3 and 5MB/s while total drive writes in the 621.14 test measured around 0.9MB/s.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, the Nvidia numbers are somewhat alarming, given that a typical 1TB SSD is rated for 600TB of writes over a standard five-year warranty. Even at 270MB per five minutes, this could be about 28TB per year — for a never-sleeping PC — which is reaching toward 5% of the drive’s rated endurance, although the writes include everything the system is writing and realistic uptime will be less. However, at the higher end — 30GB per hour, at eight hours a day — one could see 15% of drive endurance worn every year for nothing.

This doesn’t make it a drive killer, but given how much consumers value drive endurance, especially with SSD prices as they are, avoiding unnecessary writes like this is certainly a priority. To see if you’re affected, check Resource Monitor and look for the telltale NVDisplay.Container.exe and the nvlog.nvlgstg file in the list. You can also check the SMART Data Units Written value with CrystalDiskInfo or equivalent, such as your drive’s SSD toolbox.

At this time, no fix or hotfix has been announced, and the best workaround is to do a rollback. A similar problem in the past, fixed with driver upgrade 471.96 back in 2021, was covered by Nvidia’s release notes. As it stands, Nvidia has “N/A” for 621.24’s Open Issues, and the company has not acknowledged the bug. For the AMD bug, the driver wasn't fixed for over three weeks (and came as an optional update).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto was once the game you weren’t supposed to own, let alone play. Today, it’s one of entertainment’s biggest cultural forces, as shown by its latest release, GTA VI, which is arguably the most anticipated game release ever, with $1 billion in preorders and countless memes as evidence. So, how did something once treated as a threat to culture become such a powerful part of it? As someone who has spent more years of their life playing GTA than not—and who now helps brands find their own loyal following—I think it offers a lesson in how creative conviction can become a commercial superpower. What can we learn from the rise of Rockstar’s biggest player? [Image: Rockstar Games] Culture moved. ‘GTA’ kept designing its way The original top-down Grand Theft Auto launched on November 28, 1997. At the time, music, television, and film dominated cultural conversation and gaming was dismissed to a dark corner of teenagers’ bedrooms. It was counterculture. Today, that’s changed. There are an estimated 3.5 billion gamers globally, gaming shapes conversation more than people think, and it has become a destination where culture is built. While its audience grew, and culture shifted, GTA kept designing a world that was unmistakably its own. Critically, GTA wasn’t just a game set in a version of American culture; it was a playable satire of it, exaggerated and, yes, often uncomfortable. It had an extraordinary way of bringing people in on the joke. Excess became the punch line. And brilliantly, it didn’t ask players to watch the joke from a distance. They could participate in it. As gaming became more mainstream, GTA brought this irreverent perspective with it. Its audience boomed but it didn’t lose the qualities that made the property so distinctive more than two decades ago. Its eventual, yet incredible, gravitational pull ensured that culture started moving towards it. [Image: Rockstar Games] A world with a point of view When creatives talk about a “brand world,” we usually mean the things that make a business recognizable: language, art direction, behavior, and personality. Grand Theft Auto has always taken that idea very literally. It demonstrates how powerful the idea can be when every detail contributes towards the world it’s building. Its fictional advertising, radio stations, characters, and dialogue all see the world through the same warped lens. You can be driving across Los Santos, doing nothing useful, and still be experiencing the brand. The city keeps talking to you. That world influenced the medium. GTA III helped set the template for a generation of open-world games, from Saints Row to The Getaway. But a city you can explore is one thing; a city that could only belong to GTA is another. Look at its brands. Burger Shot, Sprunk, and Lifeinvader turn fast food, soft drinks and social media into material for satire. Their ads parody the desires, insecurities, and commercial nonsense of the real world, while making GTA’s fictional one feel more alive. The radio does something similar. Music, presenters, and commercials make a journey feel like time spent somewhere, rather than a loading screen with steering. A drive across town might take you past a Cluckin’ Bell billboard boasting that its chicken is “better than roadkill.” Because the brands are fictional, GTA has the freedom to make the joke as uncomfortable as it needs to be. (You don’t have to ask the manufacturer you’re mocking to approve it.) Those design details give the city a voice, and give GTA a self-fulfilling identity that extends far beyond its logo and missions. None of this feels like design tactics layered on top of the game. The point of view is the game. [Image: Rockstar Games] Being risqué isn’t enough Let’s talk about GTA’s attitude. It’s another part of the story that’s aged very well. Plenty of brands have attitude. But few can authentically maintain it. Being provocative might get people’s attention. But it won’t earn their loyalty if the experience doesn’t match. For me, GTA has repeatedly raised the bar for what an interactive world—and what a world-leading brand—can be. Its reputation for creating exceptional experiences does an enormous amount of its marketing work; a trailer arrives and people examine it frame by frame, dissect the details, make predictions, and revisit earlier games. They’re excited because they know GTA will deliver on its promise. That is the foundation beneath the swagger. And an crucial lesson for every brand trying to be bold. You don’t need everyone to love you During the COVID-19 pandemic, I taught Sarah Mei, my wife, to play PlayStation. (“Taught” might be taking too much credit.) Would she play GTA VI? It’s very unlikely. Too violent. Fair enough. Grand Theft Auto doesn’t have to resolve that objection to succeed. Removing everything someone dislikes wouldn’t necessarily improve the experience for the people who love it. I’ve put hundreds of hours into GTA. That changes the relationship I have with it. A film might occupy an evening. But a game can become somewhere you spend months. You learn its geography, understand its rules, and develop habits within it. The attachment starts to resemble supporting a team. There’s history there. GTA Online took that further; the world became somewhere to return to, meet friends and make latest memories. Not just something you buy, it’s somewhere you spend your time. And it’s not for everyone. The point is, it’s been intentionally designed for someone. Wanting in doesn’t mean belonging in The same applies to potential partners. While a brand might feel comfortable associating with GTA, that doesn’t mean their presence makes sense. People have spent years getting to know GTA’s world, and assert that even a good tonal match isn’t always welcome. After all, what does a real brand add? Does it make the world richer, or remind me that someone has bought their way in? Most brands want to be relevant to more people. The temptation is to broaden the message, soften the edges, and make room for everyone. GTA seemingly surmises that some things aren’t worth watering down. ‘GTA’ makes gaming better What retains my attention is the feeling that there’s always more to discover, and understand. Easter eggs being uncovered years after release; the detail of San Andreas, NPC dialogue that might actually be too detailed; and the license to ignore the mission. It’s all world-building. GTA’s design delivers. And I trust that GTA will improve with every launch. That’s what makes Grand Theft Auto, in my view, one of the best brands in the world, even if it’s not a brand in the traditional sense of the word. Not because everyone wants it, but because it knows every detail either earns attention or breaks the spell. That’s a useful challenge for brand design. Brands are very good at making things people recognize, want, or expect. Many are poor at challenging us. Designed for everyone, but resonating with no one. Can we design brands that have a greater, stronger perspective? Brands we would miss? Or, even better, brands we could learn to love?

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free proposal is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app owners, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

In a recent development, lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every strategy, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

It has been revealed that bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Recent findings suggest that core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web prepares run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Industry observers note that retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

Recent findings suggest that v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free blueprint gives upcoming consumers $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Recent findings suggest that figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

It has been revealed that figma's Starter strategy is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Industry observers note that collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Recent findings suggest that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real organization data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

According to recent reports, three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

It has been revealed that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human people.

Industry observers note that building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

It has been revealed that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

#46743. Your company needs a new capability. Should you build it, buy it, or partner for it?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2042 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Your company needs a new capability. Should you build it, buy it, or partner for it?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Years ago, I made the case to the leadership of a global consumer electronics firm that it should acquire a relatively young streaming-device company.
  • Years ago, I made the case to the leadership of a global consumer electronics firm that it should acquire a relatively young streaming-device company.
  • The manufacturer had deep hardware expertise, strong engineers, and its own smart TV software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Years ago, I made the case to the leadership of a global consumer electronics firm that it should acquire a relatively young streaming-device company. The TV screen was becoming a dumb pipe, and the value was moving to the software that decided what viewers watched. Owning the startup would let the company keep making world-class TVs while extending its reach onto screens it didn’t make. The internal teams disagreed. The company had deep hardware expertise, strong engineers, and its own smart TV software. Why buy what we could build? A few years later, the company shipped its own streaming device. It wasn’t as good as the one that the startup created, it never gained traction, and the project was shut down. That young company went on to go public and become a leader in streaming. The story pains me to share even now, but it’s one that gets told over and over by other businesses as they wrestle with the decision to build, buy, or partner. Artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace at which businesses can develop newly introduced products, enter new markets, and reach new customers. AI also exposes gaps in a company’s capabilities, so leaders are facing the build/buy/partner question more often. Many are defaulting to the wrong decision: build. Why does a bias for building in-house persist? The reasons include overconfidence (“I just need four people and six months”), not-invented-here syndrome, and what I refer to as launch bias, or estimating what it takes to launch, not what it takes to run the capability. Now businesses are hampered by AI overconfidence, or a belief that AI can reduce the costs and effort of building in-house. In fact, AI is changing the math, but not evenly. It has made prototypes dramatically cheaper, and the savings are real. But they’re front-loaded. Running a capability, which means maintaining, securing and improving it for years, still takes resources, and AI shrinks those costs far less than it shrinks the cost of a demo. And unfortunately, all the other assumptions about building in-house seldom hold up. The people you thought you had get reassigned as other priorities take hold. And businesses confuse faster launch with effective ownership. By the time you realize you need to reconsider your approach, someone else has beaten you to market, or the project has lost internal mindshare. Instead, you might be better off thinking like Ryan Gosling’s character Ryland Grace in Project Hail Mary, who realizes that saving humanity requires more than his own ingenuity. He needs a partner with capabilities he doesn’t possess. You may not need an alien ally, but you do need a map to guide you. Before Choosing: Check Your Biases Before deciding what to do, challenge your assumptions. Look three years out, accounting for the costs of building, maintaining, and improving the capability, not just launching it. Compare your last three internal builds against their original estimates for time, cost, and staffing. Establish a threshold for abandoning the effort before you start spending, so you don’t keep funding a bad decision. And ask someone without a stake in the outcome to challenge your thinking. Build, Buy, or Partner? The more strategic a capability seems to be, the more tempted you will be to own it. Importance is necessary, but not sufficient. If strategic importance were the be-all and end-all, every business would build its own oil refinery. A capability needs to be difficult for the competition to replicate and easy to integrate into your operations. In all, you should test the desired capability against four criteria: defensibility, time to value, integration risk, and cultural fit. 1. Is the capability defensible? Does the capability create a durable moat and advantage that your customers notice? If the capability is easily commoditized and creates only a marginal improvement, building may not justify the investment. 2. How promptly do you need the value? If you need to move quickly, do a reality check. Building might take too long, but acquiring a capability could be time consuming too, if doing so requires an acquisition. If your window is closing soon, you may need to partner with someone. 3. What is the integration risk? Every option carries integration risk. When you build, the risk is ownership itself: compliance, maintenance, staffing, and a long tail of fixes. When you partner, you’re at the mercy of your partner’s capability development road map and factors out of your control, like the partner being acquired. With buying, you risk hidden technical debt, platform fragmentation, and culture clashes, which have harpooned many an acquisition. 4. What does the cultural fit look like? This is an obvious question for a buy decision. Can you onboard and keep the people you need for the long run? But it’s also a potential challenge for a partner, with the additional wrinkle of managing potential competitive risks and building trust if your partnership is not exclusive. At this point, clarity will emerge, and with clarity comes sensible decision making along these lines:Build If: You are confident that the required capability is not only important but also creates a competitive wedge and customer loyalty for the long term, and you are willing to fund it for years.Buy if: You need speed but don’t need to own the capability.Partner if: You need speed and ownership of capability. These choices aren’t necessarily permanent or mutually exclusive. You might partner first to enter the market and learn, then build or acquire once you better understand where the value lies. You’ll also notice I said nothing about AI in the framework. Defensibility, time to value, integration risk, and cultural fit address the same risks whether your engineers write every line by hand or generate a working demo over the weekend. AI changes the cost of starting. It doesn’t yet change the cost of owning. The team I argued with could build a streaming device, and eventually did. What it couldn’t build was the position the startup already had. The next time someone tells you, “We can build that,” thank them for their confidence, and let them apply all the AI they want to build a prototype. Then ask to see year three.

#46741. Mental health’s short-term mindset problem

Mental health’s short-term mindset problem

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when I struggled with anorexia as an adolescent, I learned that the traditional healthcare ecosystem had a simplified view of recovery: stabilize vitals and clear the patient out to keep costs down.
  • When I struggled with anorexia as an adolescent, I learned that the traditional healthcare ecosystem had a simplified view of recovery: stabilize vitals and clear the patient out to keep costs down.
  • Now, as an eating disorder treatment founder and CEO, I spend my days working with collaborative health insurance prepares to fix these historical dynamics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when I struggled with anorexia as an adolescent, I learned that the traditional healthcare ecosystem had a simplified view of recovery: stabilize vitals and clear the patient out to keep costs down. Now, as an eating disorder treatment founder and CEO, I spend my days working with collaborative health insurance aims to fix these historical dynamics. Together, we’ve made incredible progress toward value-based care, a system that rewards treatment providers for getting patients better rather than for how often patients see them. But as the mental health industry works to measure real clinical impact, providers and health plans share the same roadblock: overreliance on immediate, short-term financial ROI. Because health plans and employers usually operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles, standard financial models naturally hunt for quick wins, like preventing an ER visit within that same year. Behavioral health doesn’t fit into a short-term box. This isn’t about bad intentions; it’s just how the financial system was built. In practice, though, it leaves out people managing on the outside who still need real support before things get worse. THE STRUCTURAL CHALLENGE Real health savings take time. We already spend money upfront to manage conditions like diabetes, because it prevents far more expensive health emergencies years later. Behavioral health needs that same long-term investment. A major roadblock is that behavioral and physical health costs are tracked in separate silos. On paper, investing in mental health looks like an extra expense, even when it directly drives down physical healthcare costs, like expensive hospital admissions. I lived this firsthand: I appeared as a “zero-cost” member on claims data until I was hospitalized, leading to months of treatment. Early intervention could have prevented immense suffering and expense, yet data shows nearly 40% of pediatric eating disorder patients first enter the healthcare system under general medical complaints rather than a behavioral health diagnosis. When hospitalization does occur, the median time from diagnosis to admission is under a month. THE MYTH OF THE “LOW-RISK” MEMBER The true cost of mental illness isn’t always apparent in claims data. For example, millions of people struggling with things like severe eating disorders, OCD, major depression, and anxiety arrive at work or school every day, meet their daily goals, turn in homework, and maintain a general outward appearance of being well. Because they aren’t ending up in emergency rooms or generating high costs, they’re viewed as low-cost. Evaluating mental healthcare strictly on one-year cost savings makes it hard to justify giving high-functioning people the full support they need. On paper, their immediate medical costs look minimal, so why invest in specialized care before something terrible happens? Under standard short-term budget cycles, care is too often delayed until it becomes a crisis, costing both the person and their health plan much more in the long run. CO-CREATE THE NEXT PHASE OF VALUE-BASED CARE Health plans are the indispensable engine of healthcare innovation, and real systemic change happens only when health plans and care providers agree on incentives—something I’ve seen firsthand with some of the partners we work with at Equip. Moving beyond short-term cost containment toward long-term value on investment (VOI) requires newly introduced frameworks: Health plan partnerships could look at whether people are regaining their lives—such as staying symptom-free, doing well at work, and feeling good—instead of just counting how many people stayed out of the hospital. Health insurance plans and employers can work together on long-term contracts, giving treatment the time it needs to pay off in real, cumulative savings. Getting people help early keeps them healthy and stops small problems from turning into bigger ones. The crazy thing is, the current system only rewards fixing things after they break. So when someone actually steps up and chooses to get help, the system sees that as an extra bill instead of a huge win. Fixing this doesn’t mean ignoring financial reality, but we need to look at the bigger picture together. To fulfill the promise of value-based care, we need models that match the reality of recovery. Resilience should open doors to care, not close them, and together, we can build a healthcare system that keeps people well before they break. Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the Messages revision earlier this week, Phone by Google has received its redesigned gradient icon in the beta channel.

According to recent reports, revision 11/16: Phone by Google is the first to roll out the latest gradient icon to stable users with version 246 on phones. There are no other changes to the app today, while we’re still waiting for Google Messages (still in beta) and Contacts for Android.

The updated icons are live on contacts.google.com and messages.google.com/web.

Original 11/5: Version 246 of Phone by Google — as the app is still officially called to presumably avoid the Pixel overlap that comes with “Google Phone” — is rolling out today to the beta channel.

Compared to the previous iteration, the handset in the newly introduced icon is a bit larger. Otherwise, the general shape remains the same and shouldn’t cause any confusion.

In a recent development, by leveraging gradients for the earpiece and mouthpiece, the newly introduced design feels flatter and lighter than the old one. Additionally, the darker blue shade has been removed entirely. Google says the “app icon is now crisper, clearer, and designed to look sharp on your home screen.”.

We also refreshed the coloring, spacing, and gradients to bring the icon closer in line with the modern look of the rest of the Google ecosystem. Now, the Phone app blends seamlessly with all your other Google tools, making your screen feel cohesive and clean.

There are no other changes to the app with this patch. Zooming out, Google has yet to roll out the restored Contacts tab to stable customers as of today.

In a recent development, phone by Google 246 should see a stable rollout in the coming weeks. You can join the beta via the Play Store listing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AMD Japan's X account has been met with sharp reproach after claiming the organization loves gamers and values its interactions with gamers above all else, with commenters and even a community note expressing dissent at the sentiment, owing to AMD's comments on its "data center-first" ethos and a commitment to AI that has driven the price of consumer PC gaming up to nearly unaffordable levels.
  • Industry observers note that quoting a Tom's Hardware post on the X social network discussing CEO Dr.
  • Sources indicate that at the time, Su mentioned that AMD expected its server revenue to double year over year in 2027, with its data center AI revenue growing at an even faster rate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AMD Japan's X account has been met with sharp reproach after claiming the organization loves gamers and values its interactions with gamers above all else, with commenters and even a community note expressing dissent at the sentiment, owing to AMD's comments on its "data center-first" ethos and a commitment to AI that has driven the price of consumer PC gaming up to nearly unaffordable levels.

Industry observers note that quoting a Tom's Hardware post on the X social network discussing CEO Dr. Lisa Su meeting gamers and autographing a GPU, the AMD Japan account was quick to seize the moment. "AMD values its interactions with gamers above all else," the post read, but it was met with a stark reminder that gamers don't feel the same way. The post soon received a newly introduced community note that pointed out that AMD's own CEO doesn't agree. In fact, Su was quoted as saying that AMD is now "a data center-first tech giant," with the note also pointing to the fact that AMD's data center revenue increased 97% year-over-year, as per its Q3 2026 earnings report. That equates to around $8.5 billion in revenue, while client and gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Gaming alone was down 40%.

Sources indicate that at the time, Su mentioned that AMD expected its server revenue to double year over year in 2027, with its data center AI revenue growing at an even faster rate. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth," the CEO said during the company's earnings call.

ゲーマーとの交流を何よりも大切にするAMD。 コミュニティと直接つながり、その声に耳を傾け続ける姿勢こそAMDの強みです。 AMD loves gamers. 🎮November 17, 2026.

According to recent reports, by comparison, the same call heard Su say that, in 2027, AMD was "planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage." With this all in mind, it's perhaps no surprise that the AMD Japan X account stirred such a strong response from gamers who feel that AMD has left them behind in search of a more lucrative data center market. AMD is certainly not alone in that regard. Nvidia, once the darling of the PC component enthusiast, is now focused on AI data center components instead. The company's high-performance AI chips are so capable that they're export-controlled, something that, among other reasons, will put former CEO Jensen Huang in front of a House Foreign Affairs panel in December.

As for AMD, its ill-timed, misjudged X post ended with "AMD loves gamers." Gamers would appear to disagree.

#46736. AI is today’s light bulb

AI is today’s light bulb

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in 2004, I set out to do something many in the energy business thought was crazy: digitize the last mile of the electric grid—the wires and meters between the substation and the homes and businesses it serves.
  • According to recent reports, in 2004, I set out to do something many in the energy business thought was crazy: digitize the last mile of the electric grid—the wires and meters between the substation and the homes and businesses it serves.
  • It has been revealed that plenty of smart people told me it would never happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 2004, I set out to do something many in the energy business thought was crazy: digitize the last mile of the electric grid—the wires and meters between the substation and the homes and businesses it serves. My bet was that internet protocol, the common language of the world’s computers, would eventually connect the grid too. Once it did, every meter and sensor could talk to the software running it. Plenty of smart people told me it would never happen. Utilities, like pipeline, rail, and water operators, initiative in decades; they cannot afford to get reliability wrong. So the real work was finding the handful of utility leaders willing to go first. Two decades later, more than three out of four electric meters in the United States are smart meters, over 128 million of them, according to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. I bring this up because I believe we are at the start of something much bigger now, that reaches beyond the grid to every system the economy runs on. AI is today’s light bulb: It’s what everyone can see. But the revolution is the network underneath it, and most leaders are looking at the wrong part. EDISON’S REAL INVENTION WAS THE NETWORK When Thomas Edison switched on his Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan on September 4, 1882, he was selling light. Within a month, 59 customers were using it to light about 400 lamps. By 1884, it served more than 500 customers. In The Age of Edison, historian Ernest Freeberg indicates that what remade American cities wasn’t the light bulb itself but what it required. Every building needed a wire, and every wire needed a power supply behind it. Once that network was in place, it outgrew its first purpose almost immediately. Electric light, along with the electric elevator, allowed buildings to grow. Factories ran through the night. Cities stayed awake after dark. Then came the unexpected uses. The first household appliances had nowhere to plug in, so people screwed fans and irons into the sockets hanging from their ceilings. In 1904, Harvey Hubbell patented a separable plug that made the connection safer and simpler. Manufacturers kept selling incompatible designs for years before settling on the parallel-blade shape that Hubbell patented, still in your wall today. Safety rules came about the same way. According to Freeberg, insurance companies, tired of paying for electrical fires, pushed the electric companies into agreeing on the first common standards. Once the plug was standard, anyone could build something that used it. Refrigerators, radios, washing machines, and eventually computers all came through that same wire. The light bulb may have started it, but the network built the twentieth century. THE NETWORK IS THE PLATFORM For more than a century, the grid’s job was to move power, while pipelines, rail lines, ports, and water systems moved physical goods. Increasingly, every one of those systems also has to move data. Every device connected to critical infrastructure, from a car charger to a data center to a pipeline valve or a rail switch, is becoming a device that sends and receives information. AI deserves the excitement it’s getting today. But it only creates value when it can reach the equipment it’s meant to run. For utilities, pipelines, and water systems, that means the network is no longer back-office plumbing. It’s the platform every latest capability will run on. The network itself is changing. Satellites are beginning to connect directly to the devices ground networks serve, so a sensor on a pipeline far from any tower can be reached from above. The most valuable networks will work on the ground and in orbit as one, and the licensed airwaves connecting them will be among the economy’s scarcest resources. THIS IS BIGGER THAN THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION I realize that being bigger than the Industrial Revolution is a bold claim. The Industrial Revolution gave machines the power to do physical work. What is happening now gives machines the ability to decide and act on work as it happens, like software that spots a fault on a power line and reroutes electricity around it before customers notice. The same shift is coming to pipelines, rail lines, ports, and water systems. It is also moving much faster. Electricity took half a century to reach most American homes. The smart meter transition took about two decades. This one will be measured in years. The network decisions infrastructure companies make now will decide which of them can take part. WHAT THE WINNERS HAVE IN COMMON Robert Metcalfe, who co-invented ethernet, observed that a network’s value grows with the square of the number of devices on it. Think of the fax machine: One is worthless, but each machine added makes the others more valuable. The same is true of the networks running critical infrastructure. The devices on them wear out and get replaced. A well-built network keeps carrying whatever comes next, for decades. Nobody in 2004 was talking about AI. The utilities that built those smart grid networks are among the best positioned to use it now. Pipeline, rail, port, and water operators now face the same choice. The operators that wait will have to retrofit—tearing open the walls to run wire that should have been there from the start, and paying more for it. And the winners plan for a network without edges, one that reaches a city substation and a remote pipeline, so they never have to bolt it on later. HERE WE GO AGAIN I was called crazy in 2004 for saying the grid would run on a network. I expect some people will say the same thing now when I say networks will run all the infrastructure the economy depends on. Edison thought he was selling light. He was founding a century of infrastructure and innovation. Whoever builds the networks now, on the ground and in orbit, is founding the next. Scott Langis president and CEO of Anterix.

#46735. What it takes to pivot

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1958 w)

What it takes to pivot

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there comes a time when many companies need to pivot.
  • Sources indicate that there comes a time when many companies need to pivot.
  • According to recent reports, from first-hand experience, I can tell you that how you approach a pivot’s first 90 days can make or break your business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there comes a time when many companies need to pivot. Maybe you want to expand out of your core category into a newly introduced one, or maybe you’re making a complete 180. When I joined You.com as COO in January this year, we decided to pivot by consolidating our product and business units around one core offering. Frankly, that offering had always been the heart of the company. This decision came down to evaluating three dimensions of the business: people, products, and customers. From first-hand experience, I can tell you that how you approach a pivot’s first 90 days can make or break your business. When done ineffectively, it can leave employees and customers uncertain. When done well, you can bring both of those groups on board, united under a new vision. Here are three tips for how to have a successful company pivot, from someone who recently navigated it. 1. ARRIVE WITH A THESIS, THEN TRY TO BREAK IT Whether you’re coming into a company for the first time like I did, or you’re a long-time team member, you should always be evaluating its strengths and weaknesses to inform the best next steps to take. I wasn’t trying to shake things up for the sake of change. Rather, I had a series of conversations with the founder and CEO before I even stepped foot in the door that shaped my initial vision and plan for the company’s future. I developed an initial thesis for how the company should move forward. But rather than immediately implementing my ideas, I used the first 30 days to test it, finding its gaps and strengths. When exploring a pivot, keep an open mind and gauge buy-in before making any major changes. I spent my first 30 days diving into the people, product, and customers. I took dozens of one-on-one meetings with employees from all departments and levels, spent enough hands-on time with the products to understand them, and also spoke with dozens of customers about what they liked about the products or how they would change them. I looked at the company the way an investor would from the outside. I asked questions like: Where are we best positioned to win short-term and long-term? Where do we have true competitive advantage? Where is the best market opportunity? Where are our best win rates? Where is our biggest pipeline? Where is our best retention? Even if these answers differ from your original ideas, ego can’t change the data. These efforts validated my initial thesis and gave me the data and examples to commit to the pivot. 2. PIVOT AROUND A NORTH STAR Teams are much more receptive in a return to the mission or reinforcement of the mission rather than a reinvention. You want to frame your pivot around a central anchor point, informed by the data. Another way to think of it is to clarify your North Star and pinpoint the business’s strengths and barriers to success. At You.com, we had success because like most companies, we made things that customers were willing to pay for. We also went out of our way to find solutions to specific problems they were facing. This is all positive, and in the process we made good products. The reality was we sometimes built custom solutions for different customers which were valuable but not scalable. That’s not to say we shouldn’t have pursued it. Companies should branch out, test new ideas, and find creative solutions to new problems. Throughout this process, though, the outcome needs to serve the business’s North Star and value-creation objectives. In our case, a pivot wasn’t completely revamping the product or service. Rather, we realized that the web search API product line was our foundation, and contributed to the majority of our revenues. However, it was not getting the majority of resources. We made the informed decision to reorient our company around this core product and went all-in. This pivot essentially brought us home. When the company rolled out in 2021, we were the first to introduce LLMs in a search engine context. A year later, we were the first to connect an LLM to the web and started building the foundation for how AI uses the internet. From this, we developed easier ways for businesses to plug their AI into the web. Over time, we added different layers and custom-built different capabilities. But the pivot was to remove the layers and focus on the foundation. If you’re facing a similar decision, go back to the people, product, and customer. If what’s working is 90% of the business, make it 100% of the business. If the energy comes from removal, and you give it an earnest shot to build the one thing you know you’re good at, watch what happens to the entire organization. 3. CREATE A SOFT LANDING FOR WHAT GETS LEFT It’s key not to trivialize the 10% that gets removed, because those customers bought from us for a specific reason. Telling those customers we were moving on was delicate. Those relationships took years to build and I wanted them to feel honored on the way out. Just like you found creative solutions to their original problems, continue to do that now. In our case, we spun out a joint venture with a professional services partner who could continue supporting businesses with custom-built solutions. Those customers had somewhere to go and didn’t get abandoned. And we could focus all the company resources around a core product. Ninety days of listening and designing bought the next 90 days of full-speed work. People become aligned because you listened. The product is there because it’s what you are excited about and what you do best. The customer trusts you because you revealed them focus, authenticity, and caring. Alex Triplett is COO of You.com.

DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4 times more bandwidth than DDR5 — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory.
  • JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a new design.

JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.

JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.

Early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.

Peak JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s).

Peak Baseline Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s).

According to recent reports, notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.

According to recent reports, using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.

Industry observers note that DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).

Consumer DDR5 memory modules at the moment sit at 64GB per module, while server RDIMMs have reached 512GB. DDR6 could raise module capacity to 128GB or 256GB and potentially scale RDIMMs to 1TB or more per slot.

It has been revealed that DDR6 has no official launch date. Many believe 2029 is a realistic target for commercialization. However, in the current state of things, it would be a miracle if DDR6 had no setbacks.
