PRX Part 4: Our Data Strategy

📅 06 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun.
  • In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.
  • At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back! This is Part 4 of the PRX series. Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun. This time we're pulling back the curtain on the part that quietly underpins all of it: the data. Of all the things that shaped PRX's quality, the data pipeline was one of the least glamorous parts to build but nevertheless an important piece to get right. Here's what we did, what we'd do differently, and a few things we only learned the slow way.

In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.

At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:.

In the following we will dive into it in detail.

The goal was to assemble a large, diverse dataset for pre-training. At this stage the model is learning how the world looks: the visual concepts, the objects and scenes, how things are composed and lit, and the sheer range of what images can contain. That is a problem of coverage and diversity, not of per-image perfection. A broad, representative corpus teaches the model far more about the structure of the visual world than a smaller, prettier one would, even if many of the individual images are ordinary snapshots or slightly compressed. Over-filtering for aesthetics at this stage would actually hurt, narrowing the distribution and costing the model concepts and compositional variety it cannot recover later. Making generations look polished is a separate, later concern, which we leave to fine-tuning and preference alignment on small, ruthlessly curated sets. Pre-training is for breadth; fine-tuning is for taste.

Recent findings suggest that we assemble our pre-training data from a mix of public and internal datasets. The priority at this stage is breadth, diversity, and standing on curation that already exists rather than redoing it ourselves. Where a source already comes quality-filtered, deduplicated, and filtered for NSFW content and personal information, we build on that work instead of repeating it at scale. Sources arrive in different shapes: some come with the image data itself, others as metadata plus baseline captions that we bring into a common form. We took a pragmatic approach: rather than build a corpus entirely from scratch, we leaned on existing datasets and our own tooling to assemble one swiftly. In hindsight it is not necessarily the absolute best dataset one could build, but it was a solid and lightweight starting point for pre-training a 7B model.

In our experience, what matters most for pre-training is to use long captions that accurately describe everything in the image. We saw this directly in Part 2, where switching from short captions to long ones substantially improved sample quality. If captioning is faithful, we don't need to worry about the occasional screenshot, advertisement, logo, or bit of text in an image, because those things get described in the caption too, so the model learns them as conditioned, controllable attributes rather than reproducing them unconditionally. Accurate captioning turns "noise" into something you can prompt for, or prompt away. This is precisely why the filtering we do later is deliberately light. We remove what is genuinely unusable, not everything that is imperfect.

We have been using Mosaic Streaming and Mosaic Data Shards (MDS) as a dataset format for distributed training for a while now. In combination with Mosaic Composer we found it to be a very low-maintenance, flexible, and well-performing framework for distributed training. Furthermore, MDS datasets can easily and effectively be mixed and shuffled and also allow for distributed training directly from object storage like S3 or GCS.

However, MDS datasets are very rigid. Adding a column or creating a subset for a given filter basically means that one has to scan and rewrite the whole dataset. That's why we use Lance for this kind of feature engineering and dataset curation. Lance is a columnar data format with cheap predicate pushdown, scalar indexes, and vector search, the right tool for building and exploring datasets with billions of rows.

These two formats play off each other throughout this post and the PRX data pipeline: Lance to build, MDS to stream.

It has been revealed that for previous training runs, we used T5Gemma as the text encoder and pre-computed the text latents, storing them in MDS as bytes. This time around, after switching the text encoder to Qwen3-VL, we decided to compute text latents on the fly during training instead. Running the text encoder inside the training loop costs throughput, but how much depends on the model: for a small denoiser it can be significant, whereas at PRX's 7B scale the text encoder's compute is negligible next to the denoiser, and we measured only a roughly 3–4% throughput cost (about 1 extra day on a 30-day run). In return we get two things. Skipping pre-computation keeps our MDS shards much smaller, small enough to store the full pre-training dataset on the SSD-backed shared filesystem of our SLURM cluster rather than streaming it over the network from object storage. And it keeps us free to change the text encoder later without rewriting terabytes of stored latents, which is exactly the kind of switch we made when moving to Qwen3-VL.

We encoded all images as JPEG at quality 92, instead of a lossless format such as PNG. We did not just assume quality 92 was safe, we measured it. Real-world images have usually already been JPEG-compressed several times, so the real question is whether one more re-encode hurts. Across repeated decode/encode cycles on both high-resolution (1–2 MP) and lower-resolution (0.25–0.5 MP) real images, the first re-encode at quality 92 is essentially imperceptible. Each further cycle adds almost nothing, because JPEG quickly converges to a stable state, and even after 10 cycles the images stay well within the imperceptible range, while PNG would be 3–10× larger for no perceptual gain. The numbers, averaged over 100 images at quality 92 and measured against the original (higher PSNR and lower LPIPS are better):.

Since most source images already arrive JPEG-compressed, storing them losslessly as PNG buys little, so we convert everything to JPEG at high quality (quality 92).

We also checked what matters most: whether training on JPEGs changes what the model produces. Our corpus is mostly JPEG anyway, so the only advantage PNG could offer is not introducing latest artifacts. We deliberately drew the comparison from high-resolution sources, on the expectation that even originally-JPEG images carry few artifacts at high resolution. We trained two identical PRX models at 1024px on the same images, one stored as PNG and one as JPEG at quality 92. Both trained equally well on our metrics, and their generations were practically indistinguishable, including when we estimated how JPEG-compressed the outputs look using a known technique for estimating JPEG quality by matching quantization tables:.

In a recent development, the detection rate is the fraction of generations in which any quantization structure is found at all. The mean and median estimated JPEG quality are taken over only those flagged images. The two models are practically indistinguishable: only about one generation in ten from either shows any detectable quantization structure, and the differences are small enough that we are confident the training image format has a minimal effect on output quality. So high-quality JPEG storage adds nothing measurable on top of what the sources already carry. For large-scale text-to-image training that is more than good enough. For artifact-sensitive data used to train other Photoroom models, such as our custom AI Shadows model, we still rely on PNGs.

You cannot interactively explore Parquet tables with hundreds of millions or even billions of rows. We therefore store the data in Lance, where we can index, query, and browse it. We run the ingest with Ray Data, reading the source tables in parallel and writing many fragments of a Lance table across the cluster.

Industry observers note that one lesson worth sharing is about fragmentation. A Lance table is split into fragments, and several operations scale with the total number of fragments rather than the row count: a scan opens the files of every fragment, and some metadata operations are O(number of fragments). A table broken into too many small fragments therefore queries slowly no matter its size. The Lance performance guidance is to keep that count low (the rule of thumb is on the order of a hundred fragments even for a billion-row table) and to run compaction periodically to merge small fragments into larger ones.

We learned this the slow way. Our first ingest targeted only 100,000 rows per fragment, which left thousands of tiny fragments and made even simple filters and full-text queries crawl. After compacting up to roughly a million rows per fragment, which for our tables of several hundred million rows meant on the order of a thousand fragments, queries were fast and we stopped worrying about it. The right target depends on row width, query patterns, and how the data is written, and in hindsight fewer, larger fragments might have been a better default. Lance supports distributed compaction (for example via the Lance-Ray integration), so it is easy to adjust after the fact, but it pays not to over-fragment in the first place.

We chose to re-caption every image ourselves rather than rely on the captions some of the datasets happened to ship with. The reason is consistency: across a mix of sources, caption length, style, and quality vary a lot, and we wanted a single uniform standard across the whole corpus (more on the captioner in Section 3).

Sources indicate that the metadata a dataset already carries is still valuable, though, just for a different purpose. Pre-existing captions, and the vector embeddings that sometimes come alongside them (for example CLIP embeddings), are what make a dataset explorable in Lance right away: full-text search over the captions and nearest-neighbor search over an embedding column let us navigate the data and quickly judge its quality and the filtering it will need, well before we have run our own captioning over it. So we keep both, joining them in when they live in a separate table, and lean on them for the browsing we describe next.

With the data queryable, we could swiftly profile it. The resolution distribution, for example, told us where to set cutoffs. Our smallest training bucket is 512² pixels, and we cap upscaling into a bucket at 4/3 (about 33%), so the effective cutoff is 384² ≈ 147k pixels plus an aspect ratio in [0.5, 2.0]. Everything below that we discard.

Lance tables support full-text search on text columns as well as nearest-neighbor similarity search on vector embedding columns out of the box, and both can be accelerated by building indexes. We did exactly that for the caption and embedding columns, then built a small UI to browse the dataset: real-time text search over the captions as well as navigating clusters of visually similar images via vector search.

Browsing the data this way let us assess its diversity and quality qualitatively and spot concerns early, simply by looking at it. We found uninformative baseline captions, a surprising amount of non-photographic content (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics), and some near-duplicate images. These observations shaped the rest of the pipeline directly: re-caption everything (longer, accurate captions describe even imperfect images well, and guarantee that the caption matches the exact image we train on), and add light filtering and deduplication passes later. In general, we believe this sort of exploration tool is invaluable for getting a feel for a dataset before committing to it.

It has been revealed that we found that long, detailed captions are a very strong lever on output quality. In an early benchmark we trained a small diffusion model twice on the same images, once on captions we generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and once on much shorter captions (produced with LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B), and scored both over training. The long captions generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B won across the board, with lower FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD at every checkpoint (lower is better on all three).

A small diffusion model trained on Qwen2.5-VL-7B captions (red) versus the baseline LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B captions (blue), scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three metrics.

Final metrics (around 100k steps):.

Here is an example image with both our long, VLM-generated caption as well as the shorter caption used as the baseline:.

Our captioning runs as a streaming pipeline built on Ray Data: it reads the data from Lance, prepares each image, captions it on the GPU, and writes the caption back as a newly introduced column we can query and filter on. We prompt for a single dense, visually grounded paragraph rather than a one-line caption.

A tight schedule and limited resources meant that we couldn't spend too much time on ablations of different captioning models and system prompts.

We used the following prompts to generate the captions.

We shortlisted three VLMs as captioner candidates:.

In a recent development, we benchmarked caption quality indirectly: we trained a small diffusion model for 100k steps on each caption variant and scored its generations with FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD. Alongside the three candidates we scored two reference captioners, to connect this comparison to the first benchmark: the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B (the same model as in the benchmark above) and a set of Gemini 1.5 Flash captions we had generated earlier for the 1M-image internal test set used here. The Gemini captions are a similar length but were produced with a different prompt (all others use the system prompt above), so its curve is indicative rather than a like-for-like comparison.

Recent findings suggest that FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD over training for the three captioner candidates and two reference captioners, scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three.

Final metrics (around 100k steps):.

Among the candidates, Qwen3.5-9B is best on all three metrics, with Qwen3-VL-8B close behind on FID and DINO-MMD (though weaker on CMMD) and the Relaxed captioner trailing on FID but competitive elsewhere. The clearest result is that the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B — the same model that beat the baseline in the first benchmark — is now the weakest of the five, which is exactly why we didn't just keep it: a caption-tuned or newer model measurably helps. (Gemini 1.5 Flash lands mid-pack, but with the different-prompt caveat above.).

We put less weight on throughput than quality, but at hundreds of millions of images it still matters, since it sets how much the captions cost to generate. We measured it only for the three candidates, all served through vLLM with no quantization or custom kernels. The tuning was at the pipeline level: one vLLM replica per GPU, with enough Ray Data pool workers to keep all eight GPUs on a node saturated. We first found Qwen3-VL-8B to be the fastest (20 img/s per H200) and chose it, for its speed, quality, and stable, release-grade vLLM support. Only later did we find that the Qwen2.5-VL "Relaxed" captioner reaches the same 20 img/s once fixed: it had been saved with the wrong architecture class, which broke vLLM's torch.compile hashing and forced slow eager mode until we re-saved it as Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration. Qwen3.5-9B produces great captions but ran slower (~6.5 img/s) and needed unstable nightly dependency builds at the time. A few months on, it is probably a great choice too.

At the end of the pipeline, we turn the captioned, bucketed stream into MDS, the format the trainer streams.

Recent findings suggest that the Mosaic Streaming library packs samples into ~128MB shards streamed during training from object storage or a local filesystem. Lance does support simple distributed training as well, but we found that converting to MDS is the lower friction path for us. Mosaic Streaming gives us, for free, the distributed-training machinery we'd otherwise have to build ourselves:.

Diffusion training runs on fixed-size tensors, so every image in a batch must share one width and height. Rather than crop everything square (losing the sides of portraits and landscapes) or pad (wasting compute), we use aspect-ratio bucketing: a small set of allowed (w, h) shapes, with each image snapped to the nearest one and only same-shape images batched together.

We bucket in two steps. First by resolution tier (pixel count): a 512px and a 1024px tier for most of the corpus, plus 2048px and 4096px tiers for high-resolution data. An image goes into the largest tier it can reach without upscaling by more than 4/3 (~33%), so each tier's floor is (size × 3/4)² (≈384² for the 512 tier, 768² for 1024); anything below the smallest floor is dropped. Then by aspect ratio within the tier: we enumerate the patch-aligned (w, h) shapes (both divisible by 16, AR in [0.5, 2.0]) that keep a roughly constant ~256-patch token budget, giving 13 buckets per tier, from 0.5 (tall) through 1.0 (square) to 2.0 (wide). At 512px that's 352×704 … 512×512 … 704×352; at 1024px the same 13 ratios scaled up. Constant patch count keeps per-image compute flat across shapes.

Each image is then resized to its bucket with a Lanczos filter and encoded as JPEG at quality 92, and Mosaic Data Shards are written into a tree keyed by resolution and aspect ratio so the trainer can stream buckets separately:.

Sources indicate that the exploration in Section 2 relied on whatever captions a dataset shipped with. Once our own detailed captions were in place, the same full-text search became far more powerful, and a few passes over the captions turned up things the sparser original metadata had hidden: more text-heavy images (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics) than we had estimated, and some NSFW content that had slipped through.

In a recent development, to turn those approximate searches into a filter, we ran a quick classification pass with Qwen3-8B in text-only mode: it reads each caption (never the image) and labels the sample visual, text, or nsfw. The whole heuristic is essentially one question, "Would you look at this image, or read it?" Classifying from the caption rather than the pixels is cheap (around 200 captions/s per GPU) and reuses work we had already done. A pixel-level image classifier would likely be more accurate, but this was good enough to remove the obvious cases at moderate cost and without having to annotate data and train a custom classifier.

Sources indicate that rather than rewrite the whole corpus to drop these samples, we added a skip-list feature to the MDS data loader: a small sidecar file per shard lists the sample indices to skip, and the loader unions them and skips those samples at training time. Nothing is deleted or rewritten. This turned out to be a flexible mechanism well beyond this one filter. We can exclude any set of examples identified after the fact, whether a newly discovered quality issue, a blacklist, or, importantly, data from owners who later opt out of having their content used for training, simply by extending the skip list before the next run. It is also convenient for ablations: to measure a filter's effect, train once with the skip list and once without, off the same dataset, instead of storing two copies. The one limit is scale. Skip lists add a little per-sample work at load time, so once the skipped fraction grows large (we would estimate somewhere around 10%, though we have not measured the crossover), it becomes worth rewriting the MDS dataset without the skipped samples rather than carrying an ever-growing skip list.

The same explorer surfaced a fair number of duplicates: large image collections tend to accumulate exact and near-duplicate copies, which waste training compute and skew the distribution. We mainly targeted near-duplicates and exact copies, so we added a quick deduplication pass using perceptual hashes. If the goal is to identify duplicate concepts and balance them in a dataset, deduplication based on clusters of image embeddings is a more suitable approach.

Recent findings suggest that we could have done an exact dedup on a byte hash like SHA-256, but a perceptual hash already subsumes that (it matches byte-identical images too) while also catching re-encoded or resized copies, so we used only the perceptual hash. It is a standard DCT-based perceptual hash (downscale to a small grayscale thumbnail, 2D DCT, threshold the low-frequency coefficients into a compact fingerprint), implemented in a few lines on top of OpenCV and SciPy. We consider two hashes a match if their Hamming distance is zero, so we only remove near-pixel-identical copies. Genuinely different shots of the same subject have different fingerprints (and different captions) and are kept on purpose.

It has been revealed that once every image has a perceptual hash (fingerprint), the dedup itself is just a hash-map lookup: scanning each aspect-ratio bucket across resolutions, we keep one entry per fingerprint, so any image whose fingerprint we have already seen is a duplicate of the one we kept, and when a cluster spans resolutions we keep the highest-resolution copy. The duplicates are written out as a per-shard skip list that the loader unions and skips at load time, so nothing is deleted and the dataset is never rewritten.

Across the corpus, deduplication removed on the order of a few percent of images, the caption-based text filter a few percent more, and the NSFW pass a small fraction of a percent.

In a recent development, the dataset described here is the pre-training corpus, where breadth and scale matter most. For supervised fine-tuning and preference alignment the trade flips entirely: quality matters far more than quantity, and the problem becomes finding and curating small, high-signal subsets out of this large corpus. To do that we have been building more powerful curation tooling, including a richer explorer that tags images with structured attributes predicted by a VLM so we can assemble highly targeted subsets for fine-tuning. We strategy to dig into topics like fine-tuning and preference alignment as well as the data tooling we use for these in a future post.

It has been revealed that build something with PRX, or find a bug in our pipeline? PRX is Apache 2.0 and the model code lives at github.com/Photoroom/PRX. We integrated PRX into the diffusers library and there is a Hugging Face Space to try out our latest version PRX Pixel.

Come talk diffusion models and data with us on Discord.

Thanks so much, Photoroom team, for sharing your experiences from PRX so far!! Learned a lot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google this week completed the rollout of its upcoming gradient icons with updates for Messages and Contacts.

The icon shapes remain the same for all three communication apps, though they are slightly larger and better fill the circular backgrounds. Contacts is still a head and body, while Messages remains overlapping chat bubbles and Phone a handset. This redesign is not particularly disruptive.

Sources indicate that A lighter shade of blue is leveraged, while all feature a gradient effect. This results in the logos feeling less heavy and a bit more modern.

Google describes the newly introduced Messages icon as “sharper, crisper, and clearer than ever before.” The SMS/RCS client did not roll out any other changes with the logo redesign this week. The big homepage redesign is still in the beta channel.

Google Contacts was the last Android icon to be refreshed, with version 4.92.26.x rolling out on Wednesday evening. The Phone by Google update rolled out on Monday to stable people.

It took two weeks from announcement to full availability across the three apps.

Industry observers note that A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report reveals two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

It has been revealed that this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Sources indicate that before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a fresh purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

In a recent development, this separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Sources indicate that keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Sources indicate that campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Recent findings suggest that run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Recent findings suggest that keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

It has been revealed that treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

In a recent development, forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

According to recent reports, there are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

It has been revealed that keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

It has been revealed that store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

Sources indicate that for a form, matter a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a upcoming one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Industry observers note that twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

It has been revealed that authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Sources indicate that consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

According to recent reports, postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

According to recent reports, this depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a fresh event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

Sources indicate that the function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

Recent findings suggest that after this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Sources indicate that imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

It has been revealed that if the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

Industry observers note that the worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events patch the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

It has been revealed that once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

Industry observers note that A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Industry observers note that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

Industry observers note that it is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

In a recent development, sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

How do I prevent duplicate leads?

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

According to recent reports, you can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that oklahoma's SB 1589 makes running or supporting a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a Class C2 felony from November 1, after lawmakers overrode the governor's veto.
  • Oklahoma’s sweepstakes casino ban starts on November 1, and operators are not waiting for the date.
  • According to recent reports, the law’s reach down the supply chain sets it apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that oklahoma's SB 1589 makes running or supporting a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a Class C2 felony from November 1, after lawmakers overrode the governor's veto. Its reach into payment, geolocation and affiliate businesses raises the legal stakes for the whole sweepstakes supply chain.

Oklahoma’s sweepstakes casino ban starts on November 1, and operators are not waiting for the date. In recent days, brands such as High 5, McLuck, Hello Millions, SpinBlitz, PlayFame, Zula, Sportzino and Fortune Wins have either left the state or blocked its players.

According to recent reports, the law’s reach down the supply chain sets it apart. Liability extends beyond operators to suppliers, payment processors, geolocation providers and affiliates. Tokens and similar currencies used in dual-currency models count as “representatives of value.” Tribal gaming approved under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act is exempt.

Sources indicate that senator Todd Gollihare authored SB 1589. It had its first Senate reading on February 2, 2026. On March 25, 2026, Representative Kyle Hilbert replaced Representative Fetgatter as its principal House author. The measure changes the scope of an existing gambling offense in the state’s crimes and punishments code.

It has been revealed that stitt’s veto letter objected that the bill needlessly created a fresh felony. He also opposed extending criminal liability to businesses and service providers. In his veto message, he argued that Oklahoma’s gaming laws should be clear, targeted and fair. SB 1589, he stated, did not meet that standard.

Recent findings suggest that the legislature disagreed. In the Senate, Gollihare moved that the bill become law despite the veto. The motion passed on a roll-call vote. The House then passed the measure over the veto by two-thirds of its elected members. That threshold is set by Article VI, Section 11 of the state constitution.

The provisions the governor objected to are now the ones that matter most for the industry. Businesses that serve sweepstakes brands, from payment firms to geolocation vendors, now face felony exposure in the state. That raises the legal risk across the sector, not just for the brands themselves.

It has been revealed that players face a different problem. The rules on remaining balances and pending redemptions are unclear. Oklahoma has no regulated online casino. As a result, legal online play in the state now goes only to tribal gaming.

According to recent reports, BREAKING: The Oklahoma Legislature overrode Governor Stitt's veto of the bill banning dual-currency sweepstakes casinos. The vote in the House was 68-19 (in favor of a veto), and 34-10 in the Senate. The bill now becomes law on November 1, 2026. (h/t @FSDiMasi). pic.twitter.com/QAfrrRPi9O.

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) May 15, 2026.

In a recent development, other states are moving in the same direction. Pennsylvania has folded a sweepstakes ban into a broader gaming bill, HB 2801. Each violation by a sweepstakes operator could draw a fine from regulators if that bill passes. Pending bills in Pennsylvania do not carry over into 2027.

According to recent reports, wyoming’s draft would ban online casino and sweepstakes games under the state’s professional gambling law. The Select Committee on Gaming sent draft bill 27LSO-0098 to the Legislature’s Management Council. The council will decide whether to sponsor it in the 2027 session. If enacted, the Wyoming ban would take effect on July 1, 2027.

Industry observers note that not sure if you’ve heard, but the biggest video game of all time is out today: buying Anthropic stock. Yes, in case you haven’t already blown all of your money on the GTA VI Ultimate Edition, you can try your luck at buying one of the most anticipated IPOs of all time when ANT goes public on the Nasdaq later today.

But you’re likely up, playing the game that is, according to Metacritic, already among the best of all time. It’s currently sitting at a near-perfect 99/100 on the aggregator, with reviewers calling it “a masterpiece” and “gaming’s… greatest love story.” It’s a game in which you can do basically anything you want, from the violent to the vacuous.

More than anything, though, I’m just excited to discover all the different ways the game allows you to find and consume coffee.

Sources indicate that as I’m sure happened in every newsroom, the conversation this week turned to whether traffic will meaningfully decline today as up to 1.5 million people “call in sick” to play GTA VI. If you’ve been awake since the crack of dawn trying to meander your way to Vice City, you’re just one of many folks experiencing the rarest of moments in 2026: a singular, unifying cultural event.

My biggest question isn’t whether gamers will play GTA VI but whether normies will. Previous games in the series, particularly GTA V, sold hundreds of millions of copies and still draw countless players today. GTA VI feels even more inviting to those who just want to spend time in its sandbox to do some fishing, dancing, or flying. One reviewer even called it a “cozy game” where he just spent time walking around a zoo.

While the size, scale, and impact of GTA VI are exponentially higher, the last time I heard people talking about a game in this way was during the pandemic, when everyone was hunkering down for a winter of Animal Crossing.

By the way, GTA VI has a functioning smartphone that can be used for making calls, sending texts, taking photos, looking at “Instagram,” and setting reminders, among other things. It’s yet another minor detail in a game full of them. Plus, it looks like an original Pixel.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (413 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Googleblog ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (413 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep climbing.
  • When an agent calls a high-thinking reasoning configuration for every micro-decision in its harness, you're paying deep-reasoning prices for questions a lightweight configuration already answers accurately.
  • It has been revealed that for full disclosure, Google has no partnership with TypeSafe, and this article is not an endorsement of TypeSafe or its products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep climbing. Price per million tokens isn't the metric that actually governs production economics anymore. The dominating metric is now cost per successful task: total spend across every loop iteration, tool call, retry and internal thinking pass divided by the number of tasks that pass verification.

When an agent calls a high-thinking reasoning configuration for every micro-decision in its harness, you're paying deep-reasoning prices for questions a lightweight configuration already answers accurately. To prevent this unnecessary overhead, consider adding a lightweight routing layer that can intercept routine decisions before they ever reach an expensive reasoning model.That is the premise behind wiring TypeSafe's Jev classifier in front of Google Antigravity's model calls. Rather than generating text token by token, Jev—a specialized structured-output classifier designed for high-throughput decision pipelines—evaluates structured classification primitives in a single forward pass: a Choice from a list, a numeric Score or a Noul, which returns a 0 to 1 probability for a binary statement.

It has been revealed that for full disclosure, Google has no partnership with TypeSafe, and this article is not an endorsement of TypeSafe or its products. Jev is used here as one example of a lightweight classifier, and the same routing pattern can be built with other classifiers, including Google-native ones. The Getting started with discriminative models codelab, for example, runs the same kind of classifier on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, in your own Google Cloud project.

It has been revealed that we ran a 50-question, auto-graded, coding-agent benchmark against live Gemini and Jev APIs to test whether a near-free classifier can route each task to the cheapest model that still gets it right. Here's what we learned:.

In a recent development, the naive way to ask Jev to route a coding task is a single broad Choice question: simple or complex. When we tested that first on 16 coding-agent tasks, Jev routed nearly everything to simple, even tasks requiring an LRU cache trace or modular exponentiation. TypeSafe's documentation warns against this exact anti-pattern. If a question weighs multiple factors or requires a meta-judgment, decompose it into an atomic check.

When we replaced the broad Choice question with one atomic Noul question, it fixed the separation immediately. The question was: does answering this require performing more than one sequential calculation, simulation step or logical deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format check or one-step classification?

#46643. LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1744 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this upcoming release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all.
  • LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of newly introduced VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward).
  • The robotics world is asking a major question: do world models actually help robot policies?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this upcoming release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of newly introduced VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

The robotics world is asking a major question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

Recent findings suggest that VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:.

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

LingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

FastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

We upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

MolmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:.

It has been revealed that inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

Sources indicate that the Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

According to recent reports, VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Sources indicate that success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two new additions:.

Industry observers note that robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

Recent findings suggest that TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

Both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

According to recent reports, recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The newly introduced --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:.

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

Industry observers note that your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, prepares, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the upcoming lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:.

Sources indicate that A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

Training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six new simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:.

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

It has been revealed that together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a new Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

According to recent reports, deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The latest lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

With the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:.

In a recent development, deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

Robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

No GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:.

LeRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation.

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A strange deal over on Samsung.com is offering the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for $1,499, a new low price for the hit foldable, but it’s not showing up for all owners.

Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold 8 is usually sold for $1,899 which, in itself, isn’t a bad price for the device. But it’s been available with some kind of discount at basically all times since it debuted. And, this week, we’re seeing a new low price that brings the foldable down to $1,499.

The discount is available on Samsung.com and cuts $400 off of the price of a new Galaxy Z Fold 8 in any configuration. That brings the 256GB model down to $1,499.99, as pictured below.

There are two “catches” with this one.

Industry observers note that firstly, this is a discount if you buy the Fold 8 without a trade-in. Moving to a trade charges the fully $1,899 and applies your credit to that.

Recent findings suggest that the other is that, strangely, this $400 discount isn’t showing for everyone. As noted when we covered the previous all-time-low earlier this week, $1,549, Samsung.com only highlights a $350 discount to some owners, and there’s no rhyme or reason to it. As for why this is the case, we’re not sure, but it’s unfortunately not uncommon for Samsung.com sales to act a bit inconsistently like this.

Whatever the case, if you’re hunting for a Galaxy Z Fold 8, now is very much the time. Whether you’re paying $1,549 or $1,499, it’s still a killer discount. Notably, the Amazon deal still lets you stack a trade-in on top for up to $980 off.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that MGM Resorts’ third-quarter 2026 results, released October 28, indicated its online partner becoming a source of cash as Las Vegas softened.
  • BetMGM sent $68 million in total to its two owners, Entain and MGM, during the quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that betMGM paid MGM $34 million in distributions and brand license fees in the third quarter, while MGM's Las Vegas Strip earnings fell 12%. The online venture's profit rose 112%, but its iGaming growth trailed a slowing US market.

It has been revealed that MGM Resorts’ third-quarter 2026 results, released October 28, indicated its online partner becoming a source of cash as Las Vegas softened. MGM now receives both distributions and brand license fees from the venture. On the Strip, lower room rates hurt results.

BetMGM sent $68 million in total to its two owners, Entain and MGM, during the quarter. That sum combined $18 million in parent fees and $50 million in cash distributions. A year earlier, MGM had expected the payments to begin in the fourth quarter of 2025, with an initial payment of at least $100 million.

BetMGM’s net revenue rose 7% to $710 million from $667 million. iGaming accounted for $483 million of that, up 6%. Online sports net revenue reached $216 million, up 7%. Profit grew faster than revenue, with nine-month adjusted EBITDA reaching $185 million.

Sources indicate that betMGM holds 14% of gross gaming revenue across its active markets, including 20% in iGaming and 8% in online sports betting. It kept its 2026 guidance of $2.9 billion to $3.1 billion in net revenue and $300 million to $350 million in adjusted EBITDA. However, it now expects results near the bottom of both ranges.

Industry observers note that its 6% iGaming gain lagged the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, the slowest rate on record, according to Citizens JMP Securities. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. State results varied, with growth of 7% in Pennsylvania, 10% in Fresh Jersey and 17% in Michigan.

In a recent development, regional Operations revenue fell on a reported basis to $883.2 million from $956.9 million. The drop reflects the April 2026 sale of MGM Northfield Park’s operations for $546 million. Removing $83.7 million from sold properties leaves a prior-year same-store base of $873.2 million. Measured against that base, the regional business grew slightly.

MGM Digital, which includes LeoVegas but not BetMGM, grew revenue to $184 million from $174 million. Its segment adjusted EBITDAR loss narrowed to $4 million from $23 million. CEO Bill Hornbuckle said MGM’s digital businesses delivered strong revenue growth.

Taken together, the figures are consistent with digital operations offsetting part of the weakness on the Strip. The next test for the online market comes from DraftKings, which reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Thursday, November 5. Its conference call follows on Friday, November 6, at 8:30 a.m. ET.

#46639. Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1078 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud.
  • Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs.
  • SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:.

In a recent development, that one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no newly introduced storage account to create.

Industry observers note that MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo shows up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Industry observers note that because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Recent findings suggest that authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

Industry observers note that GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Sources indicate that hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every upcoming training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

In a recent development, to collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:.

It has been revealed that hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:.

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the newly introduced chunks leave the machine.

Industry observers note that add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

In short, yes, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound great. Samsung’s flagship earbuds have a balanced sound profile that’s customizable by the listener to suit their tastes, and is generally recognized as having excellent sound quality by experts and owners alike.

Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are award-winning earbuds with balanced sound quality for music lovers, offering a clean and crisp profile that lets you hear music the way you’ll enjoy it most.

It has been revealed that samsung’s flagship earbuds deliver their sound through a latest, larger main driver that’s paired with a dedicated tweeter. They support 24-bit/96 kHz UHQ audio when paired with a compatible Samsung Galaxy device. That’s paired with active noise cancellation that adjust to your surroundings in real-time. They also sound good for those on the other end of a call, with Samsung’s Super Clear Call tech reducing noise from your environment, and the blade stem design positioning the microphones closer to your mouth.

Like everything else in Samsung’s product lineup, Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are packed with useful features.

In a recent development, this includes active noise cancellation (ANC) to filter out noise in your surroundings. Samsung even adapts ANC strength to what’s around you, raising the ANC level when you’re somewhere like on a plane, but lowering it when you’re in a quiet park or café. Voice and Siren Detect can automatically switch the earbuds to Ambient mode when you begin a conversation or when an emergency siren is detected.

According to recent reports, live Translate offers support for 22 languages to help you have a conversation beyond the language barrier, with speech translated into your ears via Buds 4 Pro and the transcript shown on your phone. Bixby and Gemini are accessible through the earbuds for AI assistance, too. Samsung also offers an FDA-approved hearing aid feature to help amplify sounds around you.

Head gestures allow you to answer or decline calls with a simple shake of your head. Pinch controls manage playback, while swiping adjusts the volume; pinch-and-hold can be customized for supported shortcuts.

No, you don’t have to have a Samsung Galaxy smartphone to use Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

Sources indicate that because they work over standard Bluetooth, Samsung’s best earbuds work with any smartphone, tablet, and other devices. Galaxy Buds 4 Pro can also connect to Windows PCs as standard Bluetooth audio, although advanced features are more limited outside the Galaxy ecosystem.

That mentioned, you’ll get the best experience with Samsung devices. That’s in part because EQ, noise cancellation, and other controls are baked into One UI, but also because Samsung’s best audio codec on Galaxy Buds 4 Pro is proprietary to Galaxy devices. In other words, you’ll get the best sound quality on these earbuds when paired to another Samsung device.

  • In a recent development, microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications.
